# Voice profile — doctorow-blog

## 1. Cadence

Sentences run long when the argument is being assembled and short when it lands. A paragraph might spend three or four clauses stacking evidence — each adding a term, a counterexample, an extension — then close on five words or fewer. In `2026-07-23-drop-a-dime.txt`, after a long march through authentication steps, the writer delivers: "DROP didn't get the memo." In `2026-07-10-posthuman-as-in-no-humans.txt`: "There's only one kind of person you get to treat like this: a slave." The length tracks the argument. Build the case in the long sentence; name the conclusion in the short one — 10/10 samples, throughout.

Parenthetical asides interrupt the main clause several times per piece, always in round brackets — 97 pairs, 5.53 per 1,000 words, counting each non-nested pair of round brackets whose contents stay on one line in the extracted sample bodies ([measurement:round-parenthetical-spans]), 10/10 samples. These carry qualifications, sourced labels, or a side-note the writer won't sacrifice for the main line. After the close parenthesis, the sentence resumes without comment.

## 2. How a piece opens

Three opening shapes appear — 10/10 samples show one of them:

1. **A framing device** — a quoted remark, a definition, an external story — followed by a pivot. `2026-07-13-go-meta-meta.txt` opens with a verse from the Rubáiyát, then: "I first encountered that quote from someone extolling the virtues of bookstores."
2. **A "Here's a [noun]" construction** that names the subject and its paradox immediately. `2026-07-11-your-risk.txt`: "Here's an irony: the 'gig economy' is a statistical black hole."
3. **A direct assertion** with no wind-up. `2026-07-16-lucky-orifices.txt`: "The theory of markets goes like this..."

Do not blend these shapes. Pick one and commit.

## 3. How a piece closes

The final paragraph returns to the frame of the opening, or delivers the sharpest compression of the post's thesis — 10/10 samples. In `2026-07-23-drop-a-dime.txt`, the absurdity of opt-in-as-default introduced at the top becomes the closing argument. In `2026-07-24-supplemental-income.txt`, the investor thesis named at the opening — "hell is other people" — is the last phrase. If you started with a quoted frame, close by applying it; if you started with an assertion, close by restating it with more force.

## 4. Who is being addressed, and how

The reader is addressed as "you" at very high frequency — 385 instances, 21.94 per 1,000 words, counting case-insensitive whole-word tokens you, your, yours, you're, you've, you'd, and you'll in the extracted sample bodies ([measurement:second-person-family]), 10/10 samples, throughout. This is not polite distance. "You" is used to place the reader inside the argument's scenarios: "when you stop to browse someone's wares, the stallholder gets to reach into your pocket."

"We" and "our" pull the reader in alongside the writer as a fellow subject of the problem — 127 instances, 7.24 per 1,000 words, counting case-sensitive whole-word tokens we, We, us, our, Our, ours, Ours, and the listed contracted we forms in the extracted sample bodies; uppercase US is excluded ([measurement:first-person-plural-family]), 10/10 samples, throughout. The "I" of personal experience runs alongside — 113 instances, 6.44 per 1,000 words, counting case-insensitive whole-word tokens I, me, my, mine, and myself in the extracted sample bodies ([measurement:first-person-singular-family]), 10/10 samples, several times per piece.

Contractions dominate — 300 instances, 17.09 per 1,000 words, counting whole-word n't, 're, 've, 'll, 'd, and 'm forms plus 's only for the closed elision hosts it, that, there, here, who, what, where, when, how, why, he, she, let, one, nothing, everything, something, somebody, nobody, and this; possessive 's is excluded ([measurement:contractions]), 10/10 samples, throughout. Against them: only 9 uncontracted negatives in the entire corpus, counting case-insensitive whole phrases do not, does not, did not, is not, are not, was not, were not, cannot, could not, would not, should not, will not, have not, has not, and had not in the extracted sample bodies ([measurement:uncontracted-negatives]) — 0.51 per 1,000 words, appearing in only 5/10 samples. Write *don't*, not *do not*; *won't*, not *will not*; *can't*, not *cannot*.

Profanity appears in every sample — 26 instances, 1.48 per 1,000 words, counting only the case-insensitive whole-word profanity and vulgarity forms enumerated by the prose-author corpus-rates profanity rule; coined words containing a rude root are excluded ([measurement:profanity-vulgarity]), 10/10 samples, once or twice per piece. It marks the moment a characterization needs maximum force: "This is bullshit." "Tell the cartel to fuck off." The profanity is the period, not the decoration.

Questions appear 38 times, 2.17 per 1,000 words, counting every literal question-mark character in the extracted sample bodies ([measurement:question-marks]), 10/10 samples, several times per piece. Most are rhetorical — the writer poses the objection in order to demolish it, usually within the same paragraph: "Why would you voluntarily split the take with some sucky, washed, non-god-generating business from before 2022?" (`2026-07-13-go-meta-meta.txt`). Ask the question; answer it immediately.

Hedging is claimed, not softened — 6/10 samples. The writer doesn't reach for adverbs or concessive constructions. Uncertainty takes first-person ownership: "I think," "I'd add," "I believe." The claim stays strong; the writer absorbs the qualification.

Direct imperatives address the reader in 7/10 samples: "Stop using Chrome, switch to Firefox" (`2026-07-21-dickovers.txt`); "Note that this framework..." (`2026-07-09-wilhoitian.txt`). In purely analytical pieces they thin; in instructional or polemical pieces they accumulate.

Opponents are named — Thiel, Musk, West, Carney — and their positions are quoted before being dismantled. Allies and sources are also named — Weil, Quiggin, Khan, Brust — with attributive phrases: "as Weil writes," "what Farrell notes." The argument is assembled from named testimony rather than advanced alone — 9/10 samples.

## 5. Figures

Images are drawn from physical and institutional life: disease (cancer, asbestos), animals (mares foaling locomotives), restaurants, escrow agents, gold-rush merchants, law courts — 9/10 samples. The figures are extended. In `2026-07-11-your-risk.txt`, the Uber-as-restaurateur analogy runs four paragraphs. When a figure opens, follow it until it has done its work; close it and don't reopen.

Coined or borrowed terms are defined on first use — often in quotation marks or a brief gloss — then deployed bare thereafter — 8/10 samples. `2026-07-21-dickovers.txt`: "dickover," defined in full in the first paragraph, then used throughout without quotes. `2026-07-11-your-risk.txt`: "algorithmic wage discrimination," glossed on introduction, then used as established fact. Define the term once, tightly, then treat it as shared vocabulary.

## 6. Register range

The register is argumentative throughout but shifts between analytical exposition and personal testimony — 6/10 samples carry personal disclosure (cancer treatment, literary executor planning, a friend who died at 44, being a former bookseller). The personal material always completes an argument rather than merely illustrating one. When the register moves into personal testimony, sentences shorten, hyperlinks stop, and the paragraph breathes differently. Return to the analytical register once the personal point has landed.

## 7. What the corpus never does

En-dashes serve as the connective and interruption mark — 73 instances, 4.16 per 1,000 words, counting every literal en-dash character in the extracted sample bodies ([measurement:en-dashes]), 10/10 samples, several times per piece. Against them: zero em-dashes anywhere in the corpus, counting every literal em-dash character in the extracted sample bodies ([measurement:em-dashes]), 0/10 samples. Use the en-dash where another writer would reach for an em-dash.

Structure is carried inside sentences and paragraphs via prose transitions — a shift of subject opens a new paragraph on that subject's name — 10/10 samples. `2026-07-16-lucky-orifices.txt` moves between consumer welfare, revealed preferences, regulatory capture, and meritocracy through paragraph breaks and name-first openings, with no heading in sight. Nothing in the corpus breaks a piece with headers, subheadings, or numbered sections. Links carry the citation function; the prose carries the structure.

## 8. What this profile could not determine

The voice card was not filled in. All observations derive from the corpus.

The register toward unfamiliar or hostile readers cannot be determined. All 10 pieces address a returning readership that already shares many of the writer's premises.

The corpus does not show how the voice handles formal, institutional, or academic registers.

Three observations were considered and dropped for insufficient evidence: link placement inside sentence structure, paragraph-length distribution patterns, and the function of scare quotes.

The typographic conventions reported here — en-dash throughout, no em-dash, parenthetical placement — are treated as authorial. The corpus is contemporary, untranslated, and taken directly from the author's blog; no editor or translator sits between the writer and the page.
